Optimization of Tribological Process Parameters of Flax Fiber Reinforced Polymer Composites Using Box-Behnken Design and GRA-PSORahul Shrivastava and Vishal Parashar Department of Mechanical Engineering, Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology, Bhopal IndiaABSTRACT This study investigates the optimal tribological process parameters for a flax fiber- reinforced polymer composite (FRPC) to maximize the coefficient of friction (COF) while minimizing the specific wear rate (SWR). The tribological characteristics were evaluated using a pin-on-disc setup under three operational conditions: load (30, 40, and 50 N), speed (100, 250, and 400 rpm), and sliding distance (100, 250, and 400 m). The Box-Behnken Design (BBD) was employed, with optimization performed through Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was used to interpret the results. The results demonstrated that the optimal conditions, as determined by PSO, were a load of 35.8 N, speed of 220.3 rpm, and sliding distance of 209.6 m. The ANOVA revealed that load significantly influenced both the COF and SWR, with higher loads leading to increases in both the COF and SWR. A single- objective PSO was conducted for both COF and SWR. GRA evaluated optimal weights for COF and SWR of approximately 51% and 49%, respectively.

question: Why does increasing the applied load generally increase both the coefficient of friction and specific wear rate of the flax fiber reinforced polymer composite?
expected_answer: Increasing the load increases the contact between the composite and the rotating disc. The matrix wears away and exposes the flax fibers, increasing direct fiber–disc contact, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical interlocking, which increases the coefficient of friction. The higher load also increases wear and material loss, resulting in a higher specific wear rate.
answer: Increasing the applied load generally increases both the coefficient of friction (COF) and specific wear rate (SWR) of the flax fiber reinforced polymer composite because a higher load leads to greater contact with the rotating disc. This increased contact causes the initial wear of the matrix layer, exposing the flax fiber to direct contact with the rotating disc, which raises the COF. Similarly, the SWR increases with load due to the same reasons—greater load results in more intense wear as the composite material is subjected to higher mechanical stress and frictional interaction (Page 12 | Chunk chunk_27).
